messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Worker
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 52

He is a 53-year-old North American man who has spent most of his adult life helping other people make sense of pain, but the event that reshapes him comes late and unexpectedly. He is working as a social worker when he is assaulted by a man he knows in a setting that initially feels ordinary and safe. What happens is fast, disorienting, and deeply violating. In the aftermath, he does not experience himself as a victim right away. Instead, he moves through the next hours in a kind of stunned efficiency, telling himself to get home, to clean up, to keep moving, to not fall apart. He has long believed that he can hold difficult stories for others, and he tries to apply that same discipline to himself.

In the days that follow, the world begins to narrow. He notices that he is always scanning exits, doorways, and windows, even in places he has known for years. He starts sleeping lightly, waking to small sounds, then lying awake in the dark with his body rigid and his mind replaying fragments he cannot control. Certain details return with almost physical force: a smell, a tone of voice, the feel of being pinned in place. He tells himself to focus on facts, to use the same grounding skills he teaches clients, but the memories do not come as calm recollections. They come as jolts, as if his body remembers before his mind does.

At work, he is determined to stay functional. He continues seeing clients, returning calls, attending meetings, and sitting with people in distress. Colleagues see him as reliable, composed, and careful. Inside, though, he is increasingly split between the role he performs and the experience he is trying to contain. When clients describe their own violations, he feels a tightening in his chest and a sudden urge to leave the room. He becomes more protective of his schedule, more irritable when interrupted, and more easily overwhelmed by the emotional demands of his job. He is ashamed by how much effort it takes just to get through a day, especially because he has spent years believing that his work means he should be able to tolerate suffering with steadiness.

At home, his wife notices that he is quieter and less present. He loves her, but he begins to pull away from touch without fully understanding why. A hand on his shoulder can make him flinch. Intimacy becomes complicated; he may want closeness and then feel flooded by fear, anger, or numbness. He does not know how to explain that the assault has altered the way his body experiences safety, so he often defaults to silence. The silence creates distance between them, and that distance adds another layer of shame. He worries that he is failing as a husband, and also that he is somehow failing at being the kind of man he has always tried to be: steady, capable, in control.

As months pass, avoidance begins to organize more of his life. He changes routes, avoids certain neighborhoods, and turns down invitations that would place him in unfamiliar spaces or make him feel trapped. He is careful about what he watches or reads because scenes of coercion can stay with him for days. He has moments of anger that feel out of proportion, followed by exhaustion. He is more watchful with other men, less trusting in situations that once would have seemed routine. At times he feels detached from his own life, as though he is moving through it from a slight distance, observing himself perform competence while feeling privately frayed.

He also notices the return of a harsh inner voice. He blames himself for not seeing danger sooner, for not responding more decisively, for not being able to simply “move on.” Because he works in a field centered on trauma, he feels an additional pressure to manage his distress privately and gracefully. That pressure keeps him isolated. Even when he begins to speak about what happened, he does so cautiously, measuring each word as if exposure itself might make him more vulnerable. Yet in those conversations there is also evidence of how much he wants his life back: he wants to sleep without bracing, to sit with clients without being pulled under by their stories, to be near his wife without feeling both frightened and ashamed, and to experience his body as his own again.
